title: John Ratcliffe released an unverified Russia allegation about Hillary Clinton
description_medium: On September 29, 2020, Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe declassified a Russian intelligence assessment alleging that Hillary Clinton had promoted a scandal linking Donald Trump to Russia. He sent the material to Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Lindsey Graham. The disclosure drew criticism because the allegation had previously been rejected by the bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee.
description_long: The claim in the assessment was an allegation attributed to Russian intelligence, not an established finding about Clinton. Ratcliffe’s decision to declassify and share it with Graham made the claim public during the 2020 campaign. The Senate Intelligence Committee had already considered and rejected the allegation in its investigation of Russian election interference. Democrats and former intelligence officials objected that releasing the material could amplify a narrative originating with a foreign adversary. Their criticism focused on the reliability of the underlying claim and the decision to disclose it. The episode therefore concerned both the content of the assessment and the intelligence director’s handling of it. The available reporting supports describing the disclosure and the ensuing dispute. It does not establish that Clinton directed a fabricated scandal or that the Russian assessment was accurate. The disclosure came less than five weeks before Election Day.

title: Eleventh Circuit panel struck down a Florida city’s conversion-therapy ban
description_medium: In 2020, a divided Eleventh Circuit panel ruled that Boca Raton and Palm Beach County could not enforce local bans on conversion therapy for minors. The court treated practitioners’ counseling as speech protected by the First Amendment. The supplied account does not identify the panel members or later proceedings, so the ruling should not be framed as a change in federal policy.
description_long: The appeal concerned local rules in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County that barred licensed therapists from providing conversion therapy to minors. In a divided 2020 decision, the Eleventh Circuit concluded that the restrictions regulated speech and could not stand under the First Amendment. The ruling addressed those municipal ordinances and the constitutional question presented in that case. It did not create a nationwide ban on conversion-therapy restrictions or establish a general federal policy. title: Ivanka Trump testified in D.C. lawsuit over inaugural spending
description_medium: Ivanka Trump gave a deposition in December 2020 in a civil lawsuit brought by the District of Columbia over spending by the 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee. The suit alleged that donations were improperly spent, including payments to the Trump International Hotel. The Associated Press reported her testimony but did not establish that she lied under oath.
description_long: The D.C. attorney general’s civil case examined whether the 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee misused nonprofit donations, including by paying more than $1 million to the Trump International Hotel during inauguration week. Ivanka Trump, who had been involved in the committee’s work, gave a deposition lasting more than five hours in December 2020. She criticized the inquiry and said the hotel had been instructed to charge a fair-market rate. The Associated Press report documented the deposition and the allegations under investigation; it did not identify a specific knowingly false answer, perjury charge, or finding by a court. title: Watchdog reported Peter Navarro violated the Hatch Act
description_medium: In December 2020, U.S. Office of Special Counsel head Henry Kerner reported to President Trump that adviser Peter Navarro had violated the Hatch Act through political attacks on Joe Biden and Kamala Harris while serving in government. The watchdog’s report was an administrative ethics finding, not a criminal conviction. The packet does not describe any discipline or White House response.
description_long: The U.S. Office of Special Counsel, led by Henry Kerner, reported that Peter Navarro violated the Hatch Act by making political attacks on Joe Biden and Kamala Harris while serving as a government adviser. The law limits partisan political activity by federal employees and restricts using official authority for electoral purposes. Kerner’s report presented an administrative ethics finding to President Donald Trump; it was not a criminal conviction. The supplied record does not reproduce Navarro’s exact statements, their dates, or the report’s full reasoning. It also does not say whether the White House responded or whether Navarro faced discipline. The episode can therefore be described as a watchdog report finding a Hatch Act violation, with the specific conduct and consequences left limited to what the source establishes. Alexander helped organize efforts contesting the election results. His statement is an attributed claim; the supplied sources do not establish that the lawmakers agreed to a plan for violence.
description_long: Ali Alexander, a leading organizer of the Stop the Steal movement, claimed in late December 2020 that he was working with three Republican members of Congress on plans for January 6 at the Capitol. He described the proposed event as a “loud war.” Alexander’s movement had mobilized supporters to challenge the 2020 election results, including through rallies and protests. The Washington Post later reported Alexander’s claims about Representatives Andy Biggs, Mo Brooks, and Paul Gosar helping plan the January 6 rally. description_long: In the days before January 6, Alex Jones said someone from the White House had asked him to lead a march from the rally to the Capitol and that Roger Stone had initially been considered. CNN also relayed reporting that Publix heiress Julie Jenkins Fancelli contributed $300,000 and Jones arranged the donation. NBC News reported that House Republican leader Kevin McCarthy spoke with Trump during the riot and described the exchange as heated, citing people familiar with the call.
